claim: Cells infected with influenza virus at high multiplicity of infection (MOI) express an average of 50,000 to 100,000 viral mRNAs per cell.
source: For instance, cells infected with influenza virus at high multiplicity of infection (MOI) express an average of 50,000 to 100,000 viral mRNAs per cell, corresponding to 5% to 25% of all cellular mRNA (Hatada et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Hatada et al., 1989).

claim: Viral mRNAs in high-MOI influenza virus infected cells correspond to 5% to 25% of all cellular mRNA.
source: For instance, cells infected with influenza virus at high multiplicity of infection (MOI) express an average of 50,000 to 100,000 viral mRNAs per cell, corresponding to 5% to 25% of all cellular mRNA (Hatada et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Hatada et al., 1989).

claim: Infection with influenza virus can trigger innate-immune sensors that induce the expression of cellular anti-viral genes.
source: Infection can also trigger innate-immune sensors that induce the expression of cellular anti-viral genes (Killip et al., 2015; Iwasaki and Pillai, 2014; Crotta et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Anti-viral response is a prominent transcriptional signature of high-MOI influenza virus infection in bulk cells.
source: This anti-viral response is another prominent transcriptional signature of high-MOI influenza virus infection in bulk cells (Geiss et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Geiss et al., 2002).

claim: Initiation of an actual influenza infection typically involves just a few virions infecting a few cells.
source: However, initiation of an actual influenza infection typically involves just a few virions infecting a few cells (Varble et al., 2014; Poon et al., 2016; Sobel Leonard et al., 2017; McCrone et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Similar heterogeneity to that observed in bacteriophage infection has been shown during infection with other viruses.
source: Subsequent work has shown similar heterogeneity during infection with other viruses (Zhu et al., 2009; Schulte and Andino, 2014; Combe et al., 2015; Akpinar et al., 2015), including influenza virus (Heldt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The influenza virus genome consists of eight negative-sense RNA segments.
source: The influenza virus genome consists of eight negative-sense RNA segments, and many infected cells fail to express one more of these RNAs (Heldt et al., 2015; Dou et al., 2017) or their encoded proteins (Brooke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus structure.

claim: Many influenza-infected cells fail to express one or more of the eight RNA segments.
source: The influenza virus genome consists of eight negative-sense RNA segments, and many infected cells fail to express one more of these RNAs (Heldt et al., 2015; Dou et al., 2017) or their encoded proteins (Brooke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Activation of innate-immune responses is inherently stochastic.
source: In addition, activation of innate-immune responses is inherently stochastic (Shalek et al., 2013; Shalek et al., 2014; Bhushal et al., 2017; Hagai et al., 2017), and only some influenza-infected cells express anti-viral interferon genes (Pérez-Cidoncha et al., 2014; Killip et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Only some influenza-infected cells express anti-viral interferon genes.
source: In addition, activation of innate-immune responses is inherently stochastic (Shalek et al., 2013; Shalek et al., 2014; Bhushal et al., 2017; Hagai et al., 2017), and only some influenza-infected cells express anti-viral interferon genes (Pérez-Cidoncha et al., 2014; Killip et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: There is extremely large variation in the amount of viral mRNA expressed in individual influenza-infected cells.
source: We find extremely large variation in the amount of viral mRNA expressed in individual cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Viral transcripts comprise less than a percent of total mRNA in many infected cells.
source: We find extremely wide cell-to-cell variation in the productivity of viral transcription – viral transcripts comprise less than a percent of total mRNA in many infected cells, but a few cells derive over half their mRNA from virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: A few infected cells derive over half their mRNA from virus.
source: We find extremely wide cell-to-cell variation in the productivity of viral transcription – viral transcripts comprise less than a percent of total mRNA in many infected cells, but a few cells derive over half their mRNA from virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Some infected cells fail to express at least one viral gene.
source: Some infected cells fail to express at least one viral gene, but this gene absence only partially explains variation in viral transcriptional load.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 5.

claim: Gene absence only partially explains variation in viral transcriptional load.
source: Some infected cells fail to express at least one viral gene, but this gene absence only partially explains variation in viral transcriptional load.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 5.

claim: The relative abundances of viral mRNAs are fairly consistent across infected cells.
source: Despite variation in viral load, the relative abundances of viral mRNAs are fairly consistent across infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 6.

claim: Activation of innate immune pathways is rare in low-MOI influenza infections.
source: Activation of innate immune pathways is rare, but some cellular genes co-vary in abundance with the amount of viral mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 8.

claim: Some cellular genes co-vary in abundance with the amount of viral mRNA.
source: Activation of innate immune pathways is rare, but some cellular genes co-vary in abundance with the amount of viral mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell mRNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 9.

claim: The droplet-based single-cell mRNA sequencing system physically isolates individual cells prior to reverse transcription.
source: We performed single-cell mRNA sequencing using a droplet-based system that physically isolates individual cells prior to reverse transcription (Zheng et al., 2017; Macosko et al., 2015; Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work describing the method.

claim: Each droplet contains primers with a unique cell barcode that tags all mRNAs from that droplet during reverse-transcription.
source: Each droplet contains primers with a unique cell barcode that tags all mRNAs from that droplet during reverse-transcription.
evidence: This is a description of the established 10X Genomics method used in the study.

claim: Each primer contains a unique molecular identifier (UMI) that is appended to each mRNA molecule during reverse transcription.
source: Each primer also contains a unique molecular identifier (UMI) that is appended to each mRNA molecule during reverse transcription.
evidence: This is a description of the established 10X Genomics method used in the study.

claim: The 3' ends of the mRNAs are sequenced and mapped to the human and influenza virus transcriptomes to determine transcript identities.
source: The 3' ends of the mRNAs are sequenced and mapped to the human and influenza virus transcriptomes to determine transcript identities.
evidence: This is a description of the method used in the study.

claim: Cell barcodes and UMIs cannot distinguish whether a cell was initially infected by one or multiple viral particles.
source: Infected cells will express viral as well as cellular mRNAs – however the cell barcodes and UMIs cannot distinguish whether a cell was initially infected by one or multiple viral particles.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the cell barcoding method.

claim: An influenza virus (strain A/WSN/1933) was engineered to carry viral barcodes consisting of synonymous mutations near the 3' end of each transcript.
source: We therefore engineered an influenza virus (strain A/WSN/1933) that additionally carried viral barcodes consisting of synonymous mutations near the 3' end of each transcript (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description in the text and the schematic shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The synonymous mutations in the barcoded virus did not greatly impact viral growth kinetics.
source: Critically, these synonymous mutations did not greatly impact viral growth kinetics (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells infected by a single virion will exclusively express mRNAs from either wild-type or synonymously barcoded virus.
source: Cells infected by a single virion will exclusively express mRNAs from either wild-type or synonymously barcoded virus, whereas cells that are co-infected with multiple virions will often express mRNAs from both the wild-type and synonymously barcoded viruses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the expected outcome of the experimental design, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells that are co-infected with multiple virions will often express mRNAs from both the wild-type and synonymously barcoded viruses.
source: Cells infected by a single virion will exclusively express mRNAs from either wild-type or synonymously barcoded virus, whereas cells that are co-infected with multiple virions will often express mRNAs from both the wild-type and synonymously barcoded viruses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the expected outcome of the experimental design, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Viral stocks were propagated at low MOI for a relatively brief period of time to minimize the levels of defective particles.
source: To minimize the levels of defective particles, we propagated our viral stocks at low MOI for a relatively brief period of time (Xue et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim describes the method used and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The viral stocks used in the study had a higher ratio of infectious particles to virion RNA than a stock propagated at high MOI.
source: We validated that our stocks exhibited greater purity of infectious particles than a stock propagated at high MOI by verifying that they had a higher ratio of infectious particles to virion RNA (Figure 2A) and to particles capable of inducing expression of a single viral protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The viral stocks used in the study had a higher ratio of infectious particles to particles capable of inducing expression of a single viral protein than a stock propagated at high MOI.
source: We validated that our stocks exhibited greater purity of infectious particles than a stock propagated at high MOI by verifying that they had a higher ratio of infectious particles to virion RNA (Figure 2A) and to particles capable of inducing expression of a single viral protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Viral stocks with many defective particles are more immunostimulatory per infectious unit than low-defective stocks.
source: In addition, viral stocks with many defective particles are more immunostimulatory per infectious unit (e.g., TCID50) than low-defective stocks (Tapia et al., 2013; López, 2014), in part simply because there are more physical virions per infectious unit (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work and data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The viral stocks used in the study induced less interferon per infectious unit than a stock propagated at higher MOI.
source: We confirmed that our viral stocks induced less interferon per infectious unit than a stock propagated at higher MOI (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A549 cells were infected at low MOI with a mixture of the wild-type and synonymously barcoded viruses.
source: We infected A549 cells at low MOI with a mixture of the wild-type and synonymously barcoded viruses, and collected cells for sequencing at 6, 8, and 10 hr post-infection, performing two slightly different variants of the experiment for the 8 hr timepoint.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Cells were collected for sequencing at 6, 8, and 10 hr post-infection.
source: We infected A549 cells at low MOI with a mixture of the wild-type and synonymously barcoded viruses, and collected cells for sequencing at 6, 8, and 10 hr post-infection, performing two slightly different variants of the experiment for the 8 hr timepoint.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Between 3000 and 4,000 cells were recovered for each sample.
source: We recovered between 3000 and 4,000 cells for each sample (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Most cells expressed little or no viral mRNA in the low-MOI infection.
source: As expected for a low-MOI infection, most cells expressed little or no viral mRNA (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amount of viral mRNA per cell among infected cells increased over time.
source: Also as expected, the amount of viral mRNA per cell among infected cells increased over time (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of viral mRNA molecules varied widely among infected cells.
source: But what was most notable was how widely the number of viral mRNA molecules varied among infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Uninfected cells could have small amounts of viral mRNA due to leakage of transcripts from lysed cells.
source: A complicating factor is that uninfected cells could have small amounts of viral mRNA due to leakage of transcripts from lysed cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference about a potential technical artifact in the experimental system.

claim: Most cells with large amounts of viral mRNA have viral transcripts exclusively derived from one viral variant.
source: Most cells with large amounts of viral mRNA have viral transcripts exclusively derived from one viral variant – indicating non-random partitioning as expected from viral infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Cells with a small amount of viral mRNA often have viral transcripts from both variants, as expected from random partitioning associated with simple mRNA leakage.
source: However, cells with a small amount of viral mRNA often have viral transcripts from both variants, as expected from the random partitioning associated with simple mRNA leakage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: A few cells with large amounts of viral mRNA have viral transcripts from both variants, likely reflecting co-infection.
source: Finally, a few cells with large amounts of viral mRNA have viral transcripts from both variants, likely reflecting co-infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A and 4B and is an inference about the biological meaning of the observation.

claim: The extreme variation in the number of viral transcripts per cell remains even after applying rigorous criteria for annotating infected cells.
source: Strikingly, the extreme variation in the number of viral transcripts per cell remains even after we apply these rigorous criteria for annotating infected cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The fraction of viral mRNA per infected cell follows a roughly exponential distribution.
source: The fraction of viral mRNA per infected cell follows a roughly exponential distribution, with many cells having few viral transcripts and a few cells having many.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The distribution of viral mRNA across infected cells is more uneven than the distribution of income in the United States.
source: As a fun point of comparison, these Gini coefficients indicate that the distribution of viral mRNA across infected cells is more uneven than the distribution of income in the United States (Alvaredo, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the calculated Gini coefficients and cited data on income distribution.

claim: Variability in the timing of infection is not the major cause of heterogeneity across cells.
source: However, several lines of evidence indicate that this is not the major cause of heterogeneity across cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript, including data from synchronized and unsynchronized infections.

claim: The sample for which the infection inoculum was never removed (8 hr-2) only shows slightly more heterogeneity than samples for which the inoculum was washed away after one hour.
source: First, the sample for which the infection inoculum was never removed (8 hr-2) only shows slightly more heterogeneity than samples for which the inoculum was washed away after one hour (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), despite the fact that the potential time window for infection is much longer in the former sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The heterogeneity in the levels of individual viral proteins was not markedly different for synchronized infections than in the absence of pre-binding and washing.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4, flow cytometry staining found that the heterogeneity in the levels of individual viral proteins was not markedly different for these synchronized infections than in the absence of pre-binding and washing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Viral mRNA expression from the secondary spread of virus from infected cells does not appreciably occur during the timeframes of the experiments.
source: Finally, viral mRNA expression from the secondary spread of virus from infected cells does not appreciably occur during the timeframes of our experiments, since Figure 4B does not show the pervasive presence of mixed barcodes that would occur in this case.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B and is an inference about the biological meaning of the observation.

claim: There are co-infected cells with both low and high amounts of viral mRNA.
source: Notably, Figure 4E shows that there are co-infected cells with both low and high amounts of viral mRNA, suggesting that the initial infectious dose does not drive a simple continuous increase in viral transcript production.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The initial infectious dose does not drive a simple continuous increase in viral transcript production.
source: Notably, Figure 4E shows that there are co-infected cells with both low and high amounts of viral mRNA, suggesting that the initial infectious dose does not drive a simple continuous increase in viral transcript production.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E and is an inference about the biological meaning of the observation.

claim: Sub-populations of cells that express similarly low and high levels of viral proteins persist across a wide range of infectious doses.
source: This analysis shows that sub-populations of cells that express similarly low and high levels of viral proteins persist across a wide range of infectious doses, although co-infection can influence the relative proportion of infected cells that fall into these sub-populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Co-infection can influence the relative proportion of infected cells that fall into different sub-populations based on viral protein expression.
source: This analysis shows that sub-populations of cells that express similarly low and high levels of viral proteins persist across a wide range of infectious doses, although co-infection can influence the relative proportion of infected cells that fall into these sub-populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Cells can fail to express a viral mRNA if the encoding gene segment is not packaged in the infecting virion or fails to initiate transcription after infection.
source: The influenza genome is segmented, and cells can fail to express a viral mRNA if the encoding gene segment is not packaged in the infecting virion or fails to initiate transcription after infection.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on knowledge of influenza virus biology.

claim: The majority of infected cells fail to express at least one viral gene.
source: Indeed, several groups have reported that the majority of infected cells fail to express at least one viral gene (Brooke et al., 2013; Heldt et al., 2015; Dou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Transcription of influenza virus mRNAs is performed by the viral ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex.
source: In particular, transcription of influenza virus mRNAs is performed by the viral ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex, which consists of the three proteins that encode the tripartite polymerase (PB2, PB1, and PA) as well as nucleoprotein (NP) (Huang et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus biology, supported by a citation.

claim: The viral RNP complex consists of the three proteins that encode the tripartite polymerase (PB2, PB1, and PA) as well as nucleoprotein (NP).
source: In particular, transcription of influenza virus mRNAs is performed by the viral ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex, which consists of the three proteins that encode the tripartite polymerase (PB2, PB1, and PA) as well as nucleoprotein (NP) (Huang et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus biology, supported by a citation.

claim: Secondary transcription by newly synthesized RNPs requires the presence of the viral genes encoding each of the four RNP proteins.
source: Each viral gene segment is associated with one RNP in incoming infecting virions, but secondary transcription by newly synthesized RNPs requires the presence of the viral genes encoding each of the four RNP proteins (Vreede et al., 2004; Eisfeld et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Secondary transcription is a major source of viral mRNAs.
source: This secondary transcription is a major source of viral mRNAs, as evidenced by the fact that blocking synthesis of the RNP proteins reduces the amount of viral mRNA by several orders of magnitude in bulk cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking synthesis of the RNP proteins reduces the amount of viral mRNA by several orders of magnitude in bulk cells.
source: This secondary transcription is a major source of viral mRNAs, as evidenced by the fact that blocking synthesis of the RNP proteins reduces the amount of viral mRNA by several orders of magnitude in bulk cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Influenza virus expresses ten major gene transcripts from its eight gene segments.
source: Note that influenza virus expresses ten major gene transcripts from its eight gene segments, as the M and NS segments are alternatively spliced to produce the M1/M2 and NS1/NEP transcript, respectively (Dubois et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus biology, supported by a citation.

claim: The M and NS segments are alternatively spliced to produce the M1/M2 and NS1/NEP transcript, respectively.
source: Note that influenza virus expresses ten major gene transcripts from its eight gene segments, as the M and NS segments are alternatively spliced to produce the M1/M2 and NS1/NEP transcript, respectively (Dubois et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus biology, supported by a citation.

claim: Current established single-cell mRNA sequencing techniques only sequence the 3' end of the transcript.
source: However, an inherent limitation of current established single-cell mRNA sequencing techniques is that they only sequence the 3' end of the transcript (Zheng et al., 2017; Macosko et al., 2015; Klein et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the technical limitations of the method, supported by citations.

claim: The alternative spliceoforms M1/M2 and NS1/NEP cannot be distinguished by 3' end sequencing because they share the same 3' ends.
source: Since the alternative spliceoforms M1/M2 and NS1/NEP share the same 3' ends, we cannot distinguish them and therefore will refer simply to the combined counts of transcripts from each of these alternatively spliced segments as the M and NS genes.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the technical limitations of the method.

claim: Cells that lack an RNP gene never derive more than a few percent of their mRNAs from virus.
source: Cells that lack an RNP gene never derive more than a few percent of their mRNAs from virus, confirming the expected result that all four RNP genes are essential for high levels of viral transcription (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: All four RNP genes are essential for high levels of viral transcription.
source: Cells that lack an RNP gene never derive more than a few percent of their mRNAs from virus, confirming the expected result that all four RNP genes are essential for high levels of viral transcription (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: Absence of any RNP gene but not any other viral gene is associated with reduced amounts of viral mRNA.
source: These results are statistically supported by Figure 5B, which shows that absence of any RNP gene but not any other viral gene is associated with reduced amounts of viral mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Gene absence does not explain all of the variability in viral gene expression.
source: However, gene absence clearly does not explain all of the variability in viral gene expression, since even cells expressing all viral genes exhibit a very wide distribution in the amount of viral mRNA that they express.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: The actual distribution of viral mRNA per infected cell does not match the mostly bi-modal shape expected under a simple model where RNP gene absence and Poisson co-infection are the only factors.
source: Furthermore, the actual distribution of viral mRNA per infected cell (Figure 4E) does not match the mostly bi-modal shape expected under a simple model where RNP gene absence and Poisson co-infection are the only factors (Figure 5—source data 2), indicating that there are additional sources of variability beyond whether cells have full complement of RNP genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing the observed data in Figure 4E with the expected distribution in Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: There are additional sources of variability beyond whether cells have full complement of RNP genes.
source: Furthermore, the actual distribution of viral mRNA per infected cell (Figure 4E) does not match the mostly bi-modal shape expected under a simple model where RNP gene absence and Poisson co-infection are the only factors (Figure 5—source data 2), indicating that there are additional sources of variability beyond whether cells have full complement of RNP genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing the observed data in Figure 4E with the expected distribution in Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: At the 8- and 10 hr time points, between 5% and 17% of cells fail to express any one of the four non-RNP genes.
source: At the 8- and 10 hr time points, between 5% and 17% of cells fail to express any one of the four non-RNP genes (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: The absence of a given viral gene appears to be an independent event.
source: The absence of a given gene appears to be an independent event, as the probability of observing all four non-RNP genes in a cell is well predicted by simply multiplying the probabilities of observing each gene individually (Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: 35–50% of infected cells express mRNAs from all eight genes.
source: If we extrapolate the frequencies at which cells lack non-RNP genes to the RNP genes, then we would predict that 35–50% of infected cells express mRNAs from all eight genes.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed data for non-RNP genes.

claim: The estimate of 35–50% of infected cells expressing mRNAs from all eight gene segments is slightly higher than previous estimates of 13% and 20%.
source: This estimate of the frequency at which infected cells express mRNAs from all eight gene segments is slightly higher than previous estimates of 13% (Brooke et al., 2013) and 20% (Dou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim compares the current estimate with prior published work.

claim: Some cells contain mutated viral genes that fail to produce stable protein even when mRNA is expressed.
source: At least one difference is that Brooke et al. (Brooke et al., 2013) stained for proteins whereas we examined the expression of mRNAs – it is likely that some cells contain mutated viral genes that fail to produce stable protein even when mRNA is expressed.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference between the current study and prior work.

claim: The fraction of viral mRNA derived from each gene is much more consistent across cells than the total viral mRNA per cell.
source: In contrast to the extreme variability in the total viral mRNA per cell, the fraction of this viral mRNA derived from each gene is much more consistent across cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Total viral mRNA varies by orders of magnitude, but the fraction from any given viral gene is fairly tightly clustered around the median value for all cells.
source: Total viral mRNA varies by orders of magnitude, but the fraction from any given viral gene is fairly tightly clustered around the median value for all cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The cell-to-cell consistency in the relative expression of different viral genes is even tighter if the analysis is limited only to cells that express all eight viral genes.
source: The cell-to-cell consistency in the relative expression of different viral genes is even tighter if we limit the analysis only to cells that express all eight viral genes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: With the exception of complete gene absence, the factors that drive the dramatic cell-to-cell variability in the amount of viral mRNA have roughly similar effects on all viral genes in a given cell.
source: Therefore, with the exception of complete gene absence, the factors that drive the dramatic cell-to-cell variability in the amount of viral mRNA have roughly similar effects on all viral genes in a given cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that relative viral gene expression is consistent across cells.

claim: The finding of consistent relative viral gene expression is consistent with prior work showing positive correlations among the abundance of several viral genome segments in individual cells.
source: This finding is consistent with prior work showing positive correlations among the abundance of several viral genome segments in individual cells (Heldt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with prior published work.

claim: Seven of the 10 co-infected cells expressed all eight viral genes.
source: Seven of these 10 cells expressed all eight viral genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The majority (4 of 7) of co-infected cells expressing all eight viral genes would not have expressed all the viral genes in the absence of co-infection.
source: The majority (4 of 7) of these cells would not have expressed all the viral genes in the absence of co-infection, since they have at least one gene exclusively derived from each viral variant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The data provide the first direct single-cell observation of the fact that co-infection can rescue missing viral genes.
source: Our data therefore provide the first direct single-cell observation of the fact that co-infection can rescue missing viral genes (Brooke et al., 2013; Brooke et al., 2014; Fonville et al., 2015; Aguilera et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7 and compares with prior published work.

claim: Co-infected cells usually express roughly equal amounts of transcripts from each of the two viral variants.
source: Another observation from Figure 7 is that co-infected cells usually express roughly equal amounts of transcripts from each of the two viral variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The observation that co-infected cells express roughly equal amounts of transcripts from each viral variant is consistent with the finding that the temporal window for co-infection is short.
source: This observation is consistent with the finding by Doud et al., 2017 and Huang et al. (2008) that the temporal window for co-infection is short – if both viral variants infect a cell at about the same time, then neither will have a headstart and so each will have a roughly equal opportunity to transcribe its genes.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the current data and prior published work.

claim: Expression of HA and GFP were highly correlated in co-infected cells.
source: As in our single-cell sequencing data, we found that expression of HA and GFP were highly correlated, indicating that co-infected cells typically expressed roughly equal amounts of transcript from each viral variant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only a single cell out of hundreds of virus-infected cells expresses any detectable interferon.
source: Remarkably, only a single cell expressed detectable interferon (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Expression of IFIT1 was rare and most prominent in the single interferon-positive cell.
source: As with interferon itself, expression of IFIT1 was rare and most prominent in the single interferon-positive cell, presumably due to the higher efficiency of autocrine versus paracrine signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The one interferon-positive cell lacked detectable expression of the NS gene.
source: Consistent with the idea that NS1 is important for suppressing interferon, the one interferon-positive cell lacked detectable expression of the NS gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Other cells that lacked NS expression still failed to induce a detectable interferon response, despite often having a substantial amount of their mRNA derived from virus.
source: But other cells that lacked NS expression still failed to induce a detectable interferon response, despite often having a substantial amount of their mRNA derived from virus (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: NS1-deficient influenza virus does not deterministically induce interferon.
source: This result is in line with other work showing that NS1-deficient influenza virus does not deterministically induce interferon (Killip et al., 2017; Kallfass et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with prior published work.

claim: Many individual infected cells fail to activate innate-immune responses even when the virus lacks its major interferon antagonist.
source: Therefore, many individual infected cells fail to activate innate-immune responses even when the virus lacks its major interferon antagonist.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: 43 cellular genes co-varied with viral mRNA expression at a false discovery rate of 0.1.
source: We identified 43 cellular genes that co-varied with viral mRNA expression at a false discovery rate of 0.1 (Figure 9, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 9 and Figure 9—source data 1.

claim: Many cellular genes that are associated with the amount of viral mRNA are involved in the response to reactive oxygen species or hypoxia.
source: A gene-set analysis shows that many cellular genes that are associated with the amount of viral mRNA are involved in the response to reactive oxygen species or hypoxia (Figure 9—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene-set analysis shown in Figure 9—source data 2.

claim: Genes known or suspected to be regulated by the Nrf2 master regulator in response to oxidative stress are often expressed at higher levels in cells with more viral mRNA.
source: Genes known or suspected to be regulated by the Nrf2 master regulator in response to oxidative stress are often expressed at higher levels in cells with more viral mRNA (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Cells pre-treated with an antioxidant exhibited less frequent detectable expression of viral protein.
source: Figure 9—figure supplement 2 shows that the cells pre-treated with an antioxidant exhibited less frequent detectable expression of viral protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Oxidative stress acts in a proviral fashion.
source: These results, in conjunction with the differential expression test in Figure 9 and the prior work mentioned above, suggest that oxidative stress acts in a proviral fashion.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the current data and prior published work.

claim: The amount of viral mRNA was associated with the expression of genes involved in the G2-M cell-cycle checkpoint.
source: The gene-set analysis also found that the amount of viral mRNA was associated with the expression of genes involved in the G2-M cell-cycle checkpoint (Figure 9—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene-set analysis shown in Figure 9—source data 2.

claim: The cell-cycle associated genes CCND3, MKI67, UBE2S, and CENPF are all expressed at significantly lower levels in cells with more viral mRNA.
source: The cell-cycle associated genes CCND3, MKI67, UBE2S, and CENPF are all expressed at significantly lower levels in cells with more viral mRNA (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 9.

claim: None of the cellular genes that are significantly associated with the amount of viral mRNA in this study are among the 128 genes that Watanabe et al. (2010) report as having been identified multiple times in genome-wide screens for factors affecting influenza virus replication.
source: Interestingly, none of the cellular genes that are significantly associated with the amount of viral mRNA in our study are among the 128 genes that Watanabe et al. (2010) report as having been identified multiple times in genome-wide screens for factors affecting influenza virus replication.
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with prior published work.

claim: Most of the cell-to-cell heterogeneity might arise from viral segment absence or mutations, pure stochasticity, or more subtle alterations in host-cell state – not due to changes in expression of the type of single large-effect genes that are usually identified in genome-wide knockdown/knockout studies.
source: One possible explanation is that most of the cell-to-cell heterogeneity in our experiments might arise from viral segment absence or mutations, pure stochasticity, or more subtle alterations in host-cell state – not due to changes in expression of the type of single large-effect genes that are usually identified in genome-wide knockdown/knockout studies.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation that no overlap was found with prior genome-wide screens.

claim: About half the infected cells fail to express one or more viral genes.
source: The most obvious form of heterogeneity is the complete failure of some infected cells to express one or more viral genes, which we estimate occurs in about half the infected cells in our experiments.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 5.

claim: The prototypical influenza virion packages one copy of each of the eight gene segments.
source: The prototypical influenza virion packages one copy of each of the eight gene segments (Noda et al., 2006; Hutchinson et al., 2010), but some virions surely package fewer (Brooke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus structure, supported by citations.

claim: Some virions package fewer than one copy of each of the eight gene segments.
source: The prototypical influenza virion packages one copy of each of the eight gene segments (Noda et al., 2006; Hutchinson et al., 2010), but some virions surely package fewer (Brooke et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Much of the viral gene absence may be due to stochastic loss of viral RNPs after infection but prior to the initiation of viral transcription in the nucleus.
source: However, it is also possible that much of the viral gene absence is due to stochastic loss of viral RNPs after infection but prior to the initiation of viral transcription in the nucleus.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed viral gene absence.

claim: Viral mutations are unlikely to explain all the observed heterogeneity.
source: However, viral mutations are also unlikely to explain all the observed heterogeneity, since current consensus estimates of influenza virus's mutation rate suggest that the typical virion in a stock such as the one used in our experiment should contain less than one mutation per genome (Parvin et al., 1986; Suárez et al., 1992; Suárez-López and Ortín, 1994; Nobusawa and Sato, 2006; Bloom, 2014; Pauly et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on prior published work on influenza virus mutation rates.

claim: The rest of the heterogeneity must be due to some combination of cellular factors and inherent stochasticity.
source: The rest of the heterogeneity must be due to some combination of cellular factors and inherent stochasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the elimination of other potential explanations.

claim: Apparently stochastic heterogeneity is a common feature of many processes at a single-cell level.
source: Apparently stochastic heterogeneity is a common feature of many processes at a single-cell level (Cai et al., 2006; Raj et al., 2006; Buganim et al., 2012; Shalek et al., 2013; Avraham et al., 2015) – especially when those processes are initiated by very small numbers of initial molecules (Elowitz et al., 2002), as is the case for low-MOI viral infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The factors driving the heterogeneity in viral transcriptional load exert relatively concordant effects on all viral genes in a given cell.
source: Our data do suggest that the factors driving the heterogeneity in viral transcriptional load exert relatively concordant effects on all viral genes in a given cell.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The virus possesses mechanisms to control the relative expression of viral genes.
source: Therefore, despite the stochasticity inherent in initiating transcription and replication of each gene from a single copy carried by the incoming virion, as long as a gene is not completely lost then the virus possesses mechanisms to control its relative expression (Shapiro et al., 1987; Hatada et al., 1989; Perez et al., 2010; Heldt et al., 2012; Chua et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the current data and prior published work.

claim: Interferon expression is a prominent transcriptional signature of high-MOI influenza virus infection of bulk cells.
source: But interferon expression is a prominent transcriptional signature of high-MOI influenza virus infection of bulk cells, including in the epithelial cell line and at the time-points used in our experiments (Geiss et al., 2002; Sutejo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Interferon expression would be more common at later times or with a viral stock passaged at higher MOI.
source: Interferon expression would surely be more common at later times or with a viral stock passaged at higher MOI, since paracrine interferon signaling (Crotta et al., 2013) and accumulation of defective viral particles enhance innate-immune detection (Tapia et al., 2013; López, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior published work.

claim: The early events of physiological influenza infection involve just a few virions.
source: However, the early events of physiological influenza infection involve just a few virions (Varble et al., 2014; McCrone et al., 2017), and so it is interesting to speculate whether rare events such as interferon activation during the first few cycles of viral replication could contribute to heterogeneity in the eventual outcome of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.
